To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effects of unsig- naled nonresetting delay on response rates can be attributed to the occurrence of hopper- observing behavior.
the response rate-reducing effects (a) of unsignaled and (b) of signaled nonresetting delays (c) to reinforcement (d) in pigeons are produced by (e) hopper-observed behavior.

the rate-reducing effects (i) occur when pecking is correlated with hopper availability, (ii) are eliminated when pecking produces a hopper-correlated stimulus that is not correlated with the availability of food, and (iii) can be produced by unsignaled nonrewarded delays.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of behavior in the production of reinforcement.
the effects of delays to reinforcement.
how the environment affects behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of delayed food on response rates in pigeons are mediated by a number of different mechanisms.

unsignaled nonrenewing delays to reinforcement reduce response rates in pigeons because they induce the pigeons to observe the hopper and because this hopper-observed time has negative reinforcing properties.
, when the hopper is available and the food key is illuminated, the probability of pecking is high, and when the food key is not illuminated, the probability that a peck will occur is low.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pigeons respond to unsignaled delays to reinforcement in the same way that they respond to signaled delays, but they respond more efficiently to signaled delays.
the effects of delayed food reinforcement in pigeons are due to an increase in observing behavior that occurs as a result of the introduction of the unsignaled delay.
the rate-reducing effect of a delay to reinforcement is mediated by the occurrence of a behavior that is incompatible with the target behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the effects of unsignal delayed reinforcement on pecking rates are not due to an aversive property of the delay, but rather to a shift in response allocation away from pecking toward observing the hopper and eating the food that becomes available when the hopper is raised.
when the food is not available, the bird is not eating.
the introduction of unsignaled delays to food reinforcement can have dramatic effects on the behavior of pigeons under a wide variety of conditions.
